claims.text: The starting material is a eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated starting alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and is brittle.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries are the primary cause of the starting alloy's limited ductility and brittleness.
A rapid high-temperature, short-duration anneal can promote in situ interfacial nanoprecipitation.
Rapid thermal annealing will form ductile nanoscale precipitates at phase boundaries within the lamellar colonies.
Interfacial nanoscale precipitates will provide additional slip-transfer pathways.
The additional slip-transfer pathways will alleviate dislocation pile-ups and associated local stress concentrations.
Alleviating pile-ups and stress concentrations will reduce microcracking and improve plastic flow during tensile deformation.
The annealed alloy will have greater room-temperature elongation to failure than the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy will maintain or slightly increase tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy will show fewer dislocation pile-ups and modified interfacial characteristics relative to the untreated alloy.
The predicted strength-ductility improvement applies to room-temperature tensile testing.
Departures from the controlled annealing temperature and duration may not produce the same strength-ductility balance.
The same improvement may not persist under elevated-temperature testing.
The exact quantitative changes in tensile properties are uncertain and require experimental validation.
